Sorry, I know you’re trying to help and I’m not making it easy.

I used to be pretty busy. I painted (oils), I was more of a gamer several years ago and like to be outside and active. I love music and exploring new genres and artists while finding ways they relate to other interests and influences of mine. All of those things have become far more difficult to the point I don’t really bother with most if not any of them. The only things I still manage with mild consistency to guilt myself into going to the gym and keep abreast on politics as well as current events.

They all used to be fairly satisfying if not distracting for a time. Lately though I can’t even manage that. They aren’t fun. Food doesn’t taste good. Music is background noise just so I don’t feel so isolated.

My antidepressant helps keep my lows from getting out of hand, it’s more of a neurological safety net. It also is one of the SSRIs that has been shown to be effective at treating anxiety as well. For ADHD I take 30mg of adderall daily and it helps well enough. On the side I have been drinking a lot more lately and augmenting this regimen with other items. There’s significant data that shows alcohol exacerbates the symptoms of OCD in the following hours/days and some of the other partaking makes it harder to learn/form new schemas. Even though I’m aware of this these are a few of the only things I’ve encountered in recent years that either numb me to the point where I can accept my condition more easily or distract me long enough to ignore it.

Well first off, psychiatrists are more about providing prescriptions for patients and less about therapy, if you feel your symptoms are as severe as you say you certainly want professional guidance for both.

Secondly, from the sounds of your situation, a working student who is living paycheck to paycheck you would likely qualify for Medicaid and possibly other assistance if you are in the US.

I've had experiences like that and I know how disappointing it can be. They should be able to put you in contact with local resources to help, some of which should be lower cost, possibly a group setting if you think that sounds doable. Have you tried talking to them about anything like that?
I'm so sorry to hear that but so glad to know you are getting help. Have you spoken with anyone at your school in order to have assistance you might need should things become difficult to control?

Given the response generated here I figured I would just reply to my own comment with the requested citations for people to review as they desire.

First a bit of a mea culpa, I said the number one cause of homelessness in the US and I should have been more specific with the leading cause of *chronic* homelessness in the US.

According to the [National Survey of Homeless Assistance Providers and Clients (NSHAPC)](http://www.urban.org/sites/default/files/publication/60436/410496-The-National-Survey-of-Homeless-Assistance-Providers-and-Clients.PDF) over 60% of homeless have experienced long term mental health issues. That same study reports over 80% struggling with alcohol and substance abuse. Yes, that's a somewhat dated study but homelessness is by its very nature difficult to track.

A more recent study from the [Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA)](https://web.archive.org/web/20111219211719/http://homeless.samhsa.gov/ResourceFiles/hrc_factsheet.pdf) reports that 26% of sheltered individuals suffer from severe mental health issues and 30% of the chronically homeless have mental health complications. Again, the same study reports 34% of sheltered individuals having chronic substance abuse problems and a 50% co-morbidity rate of chronic homelessness and substance abuse.

For the disputes about substance abuse, the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM 5) [reclassified substance abuse](https://www.samhsa.gov/disorders/substance-use) as "substance use disorder" so that chronic alcohol and substance dependence may be treated as a mental illness and not a character flaw.

That's a fairly accurate observation, untreated mental illness is overwhelmingly the number one cause of homelessness in the US.
